#4105. Fortnite's Pirate Shop Unlocks the Entire Item Shop for Free

Battle Royale tops five million concurrent players

In case you haven’t been paying attention, Fortnite is running a pirate-themed season with One Piece crossover content available right now.

But the big news is the discovery of a Pirate Shop, which makes the entire Item Shop free for two weeks. If you’re running in a squad, then everyone on your team gets the reward.

Just to reiterate: if you discover the Pirate Shop token, then you and your teammates will be able to add every single cosmetic item in the Item Shop to your profile for free. That’s potentially hundreds of dollars of stuff.

There are some restrictions: you can’t gift anything to your friends, and you can’t buy levels in the Battle Pass. Other than that, though – everything is yours.

In the aftermath of the Pirate Shop going viral, Fortnite rocketed to over five million concurrent players across all platforms at its peak. It’s a big win for the game which hasn’t been quite as popular as usual of late.

Some are hypothesising that this may be the game’s attempt to retain players once GTA 6 releases later in November. I imagine it’s something all live service developers are thinking about.

So how do you get access to the Pirate Shop? Well, you need to loot Treasure-Hunt chests (they’ve got a skull and crossbones on them) and hope you get extremely lucky. I imagine Epic knows how many of these it’s giving out.

I’m surprised something like this hasn’t been attempted in Fortnite before, because the game’s skins are incredibly popular, so unlocking the Item Shop for lucky winners was always going to bring people back.

I’ll be surprised if anyone here gets access to the Pirate Shop, but make sure you leave a comment if you do!

#4104. Review: Stellar Blade: Complete Edition (Switch 2) - Perfectly Playable, Despite Drawbacks

Though the genre has evolved and deepened over time, gacha games have historically not been praised for their depth and complexity, often being criticised for being thinly veiled gambling machines. People were understandably incredulous, then, when Shift Up — the studio behind Goddess of Victory: Nikke — announced in 2019 that it would pursue a AAA passion project called Stellar Blade. Even more were then shocked a few years later when this wildly different, ambitious project turned out to be a pretty solidly made action game.

Stellar Blade has now been ported to Switch 2 (along with some cheeky new cosmetic Bayonetta DLC), bringing this titillating and gripping action experience to the Nintendo audience. It hasn’t made the transition to more modest hardware completely unscathed, but this is nonetheless a solidly enjoyable and thrilling adventure that deserves a spot in your library.

The narrative is set in the distant, post-apocalypse future, when our planet has been overrun by monstrous creatures called Naytibas. Some humans escaped after losing the war and established a space-based orbital colony called…the Colony…from which occasional squadrons of elite super-soldiers are deployed to attempt to regain a foothold on Earth.

Protagonist Eve is a member of one of these squads and the prologue opens with her landing mission, a violent meatgrinder reminiscent of the Omaha Beach scene in Saving Private Ryan in which she’s seemingly the sole warrior who survives. Aided by a mysterious man who saved her, Eve sets out to track down the Alpha Naytiba and hopefully notch a win for the humans.

It’s a decently entertaining story, but one which feels a little surface-level in many ways. Characters — Eve included — lack depth and converse in a stilted way that sounds as if they’re quoting lines at each other, and some of the later plot twists are the sort of thing that you can see coming a mile away. Yet there’s just enough lore here to keep you interested in the setting and Eve’s ongoing journey and occasional moments of levity help to keep things from feeling too dour.

Any disappointment with the storytelling is quickly forgotten by the thrill of combat, which feels like a cross between a Soulslike and a character action game as Eve deftly combos enemies with her athletic acrobatics and expert sword strikes.

Enemies hit hard and fast and can easily stunlock you, meaning that even a single average foe can take quite a large chunk out of your health bar if you're not paying careful attention and multiple foes at once can rapidly overwhelm Eve due to limited mobility and crowd control options.

Along with the usual combos you can string together with light and heavy attacks, Eve also has a variety of limited-use Beta Skills she can use to turn the tide in her favour. You build up Beta Energy from attacks and perfectly timed blocks or parries, and this energy can then be burned mid-combo to either bolster an attack or use a flashy guard-breaking attack that can put the enemy on the back foot. This system adds a nice bit of room for player skill expression, as you can find some creative ways to weave together combos and Beta Skills to positively melt foes.

Though even common enemies can put you to the test in certain configurations, this combat system really sings when you get to one of the many cinematic boss fights against powerful, grotesque monsters. These act as occasional hard skill checks that will forcibly teach you deeper knowledge of combat mechanics as you carefully study their movesets for brief gaps and learn (often across multiple failed attempts) how to best exploit those gaps with your available tools.

Eve thus feels both all-powerful and vulnerable at the same time, which lends combat encounters a thrilling and electric feel as you oscillate between slicing enemies to ribbons with practised cinematic flair and getting absolutely folded when you mis-time a dodge. Practice makes perfect, and there's lots of satisfaction that comes from progressing across the hours and going up against increasingly more complicated and dangerous foes with sharpened reflexes and skill.

Yet progress happens in more ways than just raw skill development - there are also some light RPG elements that allow you to slowly shape Eve's build over time. Not only can you use skill points to unlock and power up new combat abilities and Beta Skills, but you can also improve stats like max health and attack through finding collectibles in the environment.

Gear can also be found and crafted to give Eve certain passive buffs, allowing you to get more value out of the playstyle you generally choose. These RPG mechanics help to soften some of the harder edges of the often unforgiving combat system, giving you meaningful ways to progress over time even if you struggle greatly with losing battles to enemies.

World and level design initially follows traditional Soulslike tropes, consisting of lots of claustrophobic halls and labyrinthine paths that often loop back on each other with unlocked doors and ladders that lead back to the nearest checkpoint. While the critical path is usually obvious and easy to follow, there are often a handful of side areas to explore along the way rife with more platforming gauntlets, challenging enemy placements and extra upgrades and goodies. This design does a great job of rewarding exploration while keeping you moving forward.

Then, roughly six or so hours in, things change up with the sudden introduction of a medium-sized open-world area, filled with quests, collectibles, and points of interest to scour. Travelling between this area and a nearby hub has both gameplay and narrative benefits, as you complete quests and bounties to progress various side storylines for NPCs living there and find increasingly better gear and unlockables as quest and exploration rewards.

It admittedly seems at first like a weird left turn after the opening hours set very different expectations, but ultimately feels like a worthy addition to the gameplay loop. And even after its introduction, there are plenty of returns to the more focused and level-based Soulslike design, which balances out the free but occasionally meandering levels and quests that can come with the open world.

Graphics look decent, but not exceptional, due in part to both the overall art direction and the Switch 2’s relatively modest hardware. Some of the vistas of the ruined Earth can be quite nice to look at from afar, but there’s a lot of muted colours utilised as you trawl through tunnels, sewers, deserts, and destroyed office buildings. Environments thus tend to blend together and often lack visually interesting landmarks or set pieces, which can make the sections more focused on exploration a little more dull.

Meanwhile, the game outputs at 720p handheld and 1080p docked, which can lead to visuals that look even more muddy due to the upscaling artifacting and relatively low internal resolutions.

Regarding performance, everything technically runs at 60fps, but there's a pretty massive caveat with that claim: this frame rate is only accomplished through frame generation. Practically speaking, this means that there's a significant amount of input lag despite the visuals themselves appearing to animate smoothly. For a game this focused on quick reaction times and granular movement, that input lag can be a death knell and does noticeably reduce the playability of this port.

However, there is an option in the settings to turn this off and reduce the game to what appears to be closer to 40fps, which feels like a much more acceptable compromise. Controls are quite a bit more responsive here, while the frame rate is noticeably smoother than 30fps. There are some drops that can still happen when panning the camera around in larger areas, but it doesn’t overly affect the playability of combat encounters and this becomes less of an issue in the many smaller environments.

All this is to say, Stellar Blade is a game that appears to be stretching the Switch 2 to its limits, but it’s a perfectly playable and often surprisingly good-looking port that accurately brings this impressive game to a lightweight handheld.

It can sometimes feel easier to pick apart a port for its flaws and what it lacks, and while there are valid critiques here to be made about the sometimes disappointing visuals and performance, it’s hard to get away from the fact that this is a ‘good enough’ version of Stellar Blade that you can play wherever you want to take your console.

Despite some drawbacks, Stellar Blade stands tall as an impressive and enjoyable action game that occupies a nice niche in the Switch 2 library. Rewarding exploration, thrilling combat, and tough but fair difficulty carry this game far and make it an easy recommendation, even if its story can be a bit bland and the visuals aren’t always up to the task.

I’d recommend this to anyone looking for a higher-budget game that favours exploration and combat; Stellar Blade excels in its implementation of both and makes a great first impression as Shift Up’s entrance into AAA game development.

#4103. Factorio's final major update has rolled off the assembly line, adding "the things we wanted to do for 2.0 but didn't have time for"

Including QoL tweaks, new visuals, and more predictable asteroids

In one of the happier endings to occur in games this week, impossibly enormous resource management sim Factorio has just released its last-ever major update – version 2.1 – on its stable branch. As previously heads-upped by developers Wube Software, 2.1 doesn’t make any big new additions to its planets or tech trees, but does sneak in more than 30 quality of life improvements and minor new features for both the base game and its Space Age expansion. Including, they say, "the things we wanted to do for 2.0 but didn't have time for." Nice to get a few final pieces out the door before it closes, eh.

There’s also an updated trailer, if you want to watch promotional footage for a game that may well have enveloped your every waking moment since 2016.

Factorio - Trailer 2026 Watch on YouTube

Here are some of those changes I’ve picked out at random. "Mixed rockets: Rockets can now carry multiple different items in one launch, so no more sending a full stack of everything just to build a small platform." Nice! "Land mines can be used as tripwires and enemy detectors." Devious! "Asteroid damage now depends on the asteroid's remaining health instead of its speed, so it is much more predictable." Convenient! Not counting how you’re still being hit by an asteroid. There’s also now the ability to play Space Age without the controversial Quality mechanic, as well as the ability to flip pumpjacks and burner miners instead of merely rotating them, like some loser.

The 2.1 update also gives Factorio one last graphical polish, including a handful of new models and a "new pump rendering system that can connect to fluid wagons no matter how cursed your station is." I’m merely pretending to be a Factorio expert for the purposes of publishing this article, though I will say – from experience building piplines in Deep Rock Galactic – that a series of tubes is only truly cursed if it still works, in spite of itself, at transporting liquids. Otherwise you’ve just got a pile of broken pipes, again, like some loser.

This isn’t the end-end of Factorio, which Wube Software have said will continue to get bug fixes and support-level updates while they largely move on to "other game prototypes/experiments." Though even if it was, it’s had a bloomin' admirable run, starting with four years of early access - successful enough to cement it as the de facto basis for later automation-builders like Satisfactory and Dyson Sphere Program – and continuing to enrapture aspiring industrial managers into the present. Ollie has over 1,000 hours in it. Maybe I’m the loser for making light of it.

#4101. BioWare is closing down and Mass Effect 5 is cancelled, months after Saudi Arabia's $55bn EA buyout

"These games became so much more because you played them."

After over three decades of iconic RPGs, developer BioWare is closing down and its in-development Mass Effect game is no more. The move comes just months after corporate owner EA was bought out by a group of investment firms for $55 billion.

"For more than 30 years, BioWare has been more than a studio. It has been a home for storytellers, developers, and the players who brought our worlds to life," the role-playing powerhouse wrote on social media this evening before listing some of its greatest hits - Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age, Mass Effect and Anthem.

"Now, after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending. There is nothing easy about writing those words. Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition."

"What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own. From all of us at BioWare, thank you for being the most meaningful part of our story," the statement continued.

Layoffs at BioWare were expected following EA's acquisition this summer - which saw investment firm Silver Lake, private equity group Affinity Partners (led by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law) and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund group together and raise $55 billion to buy the publisher. A full studio closure this soon is a surprise, to put it lightly.

A Bloomberg report also claims EA is planning to cut roughly 400 jobs across the company, or around 3 percent of its total workforce. "Across our portfolio, we're making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth," CEO David Tinson and CSO Cam Weber said in a letter to staff seen by Bloomberg.

BioWare itself has been in rough waters these past few years. The studio's live-service experiment Anthem quickly fell from the sky, and its most recent game, Dragon Age: The Veilguard, failed to meet EA's internal sales expectations, leading to another round of layoffs at the developer. Here's hoping the impacted devs can land on their feet soon.

The next Mass Effect game - dubbed Mass Effect 5 by some fans - was seemingly not ready to go into full production. Last we heard, BioWare was trying to reassure folks the game was still definitely in development.

#4100. New PS5 Firmware Update Available Now as Sony Cracks Down on Jailbreaks

Sony has released another system software update for PS5, hot on the heels of the last one from less than a fortnight ago.

Version 26.07-14.22.00 is available to download and install now, and the singular patch note makes it fairly clear what it's targeting:

These fairly minor-sounding firmware updates are actually pretty serious ones for Sony, as it aims to prevent hackers and modders from jailbreaking the PS5.

This has seen a significant rise lately, thanks to a perfect storm of contempt for PlayStation among hardcore users (no more discs), inflated prices, and AI-assisted tools that make opening up the console far easier than it might've been previously.

The situation has been gathering pace over the last month or two, and Sony is racing to plug holes in PS5's security to stop people from installing emulators and pirated software on hacked consoles.

Sony's speedy response to the jailbreaking boom has drawn further ire from the pirates, which will no doubt make them more determined to crack the PS5.

#4098. EA cancels unannounced The Sims project, trims the Skate team and reportedly plans to lay off 400 workers: "We're the number one publisher in Western HD gaming"

Respawn is also collaborating with DICE on a new game.

Not only is EA closing down BioWare and cancelling the next Mass Effect - Electronic Arts has now announced a heap of drastic changes that include cutting 400 jobs across the company, pausing development on a project connected to The Sims, and bringing together Respawn and DICE.

In a memo first sent to staff and later published online, CEO David Tinson and CSO Cam Weber first took a moment to thank employees before letting them know they might lose their jobs.

"Today, we're the number one publisher in Western HD gaming," the duo wrote. "That's an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of. Yet our industry is changing quickly. Players have more choices than ever for their time and attention, competition is intensifying, and some of our biggest opportunities for growth are beyond the markets, platforms, and business models where EA has traditionally been the strongest."

The executives then laid out some changes to its portfolio of games. Top of the list is the closure of BioWare, the legendary role-playing powerhouse behind games such as Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Bloomberg reports around 400 jobs will be cut as part of the cost-cutting changes, including roughly 50 job cuts at BioWare.

As for The Sims, the publisher claims it's prioritising something called "Project Evergreen" and is giving "the team more time to reach the full potential and vision for the game." To do so, the execs said they're "pausing development" on another Sims-related title called "Project Lotus." The early access Skate reboot (skate.) has apparently "had a lot of success," but the publisher is still restructuring the studio into a "more focused, smaller team," regardless.

Marvel's Iron Man game (the one that leaked recently) and a third Star Wars Jedi game remain untouched, apparently, though it sounds like we'll see fewer big-budget action-adventure games come from the publisher going forward: "Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success."

EA also re-emphasised its commitment to Apex Legends and the Battlefield series after the success of Battlefield 6. But that's not all. "We'll be bringing together our Respawn and DICE studios to collaborate on a future project." There's been some rumblings about a possible Star Wars: Battlefront follow-up this week, though EA doesn't give any more concrete details about what this game could be.

Then there's the publisher's golden goose, EA Sports. The executives said they're still committed to FC and the rest of its sport simulations, alongside two new projects that'll be revealed in the next few months - the return of Fight Night and a "brand-new, social-first open-world experience for our American Football team that we call 'Project Gridiron'".

"The decisions we’re making in our priorities, how we work, and with our portfolio reflect our belief in EA’s future. Some open exciting new possibilities. Others are difficult, especially for the people and teams across the company who are directly affected. In those cases, we will support impacted employees in exploring other opportunities within EA, and we're committed to treating impacted colleagues with care and respect," the executives added.

A group of investment firms led by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund took EA private earlier this summer, in a deal worth around $55 billion.

#4097. Star Wars: Battlefront 3 reportedly being co-developed by Battlefield studio DICE and Apex Legends studio Respawn

A new Star Wars: Battlefront game is reportedly in the works, and it's said to have Apex Legends and Star Wars Jedi studio Respawn working on it, as well as Battlefield and Battlefront developer DICE.

The information comes from "multiple sources" on Variety, and arrives in the wake of EA's sudden decision to lay off 400 workers, close iconic role-playing game studio BioWare, and cancel several projects. As part of a memo to staff, EA executives confirmed that Respawn and DICE are collaborating on a new project, but stopped short of saying what it was.

The report follows days of murmurings from different sources that a third Battlefront game is in the works. It started with a rumour from Electronic Gaming Monthly magazine (via Giant Bomb), which said Disney had been on the lookout for a studio to develop Battlefront 3. The names of potential teams included DICE, and Destiny and Marathon developer Bungie.

Wardogs studio head Joe Brammer then responded to the rumour on X, saying it was actually DICE and Respawn working together on Battlefront 3 - information that now appears to be true.

In 2022, EA was said to have cancelled multiple Star Wars projects in development at the time, including a follow-up to Battlefront 2. That most recent game in the Battlefront series launched in 2017 to a mixed reception. The launch version is mostly remembered for introducing loot boxes to the series that assigned random chance to earning functional in-game characters and powers. It was universally disliked. The backlash was so disastrous it kicked off a wave of legislation worldwide that deemed loot boxes to be gambling mechanics, the fallout of which persists to this day.

DICE would end up overhauling many of those systems and removing loot boxes altogether. The developer turned Battlefront 2's fortunes and player sentiment around, continuing to support the game for years, before releasing its final major update in 2020.

Battlefront 3 would be the first in the series to be published by the now Saudi-owned EA. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, together with investment firm Silver Lake and private equity company Affinity Partners, acquired EA in the summer for $55bn in a leveraged buyout deal.

#4096. Xbox cloud gaming prices revealed, with 50 hours of ad-free game-time priced $11.99

Microsoft has revealed how much its Xbox cloud gaming service is going to cost, with 50 hours of stream-time selling for an introductory price of $11.99.

This information comes from a post on the official Xbox news website, which explains that starting today, Xbox Insiders will be able to stream games using the paid service without needing an active Game Pass subscription. This comes ahead of a planned rollout to all Xbox players in November. These paid packs provide an ad-free version of the free cloud gaming service revealed earlier this year.

The full suite of introductory prices are as follows:

It's worth noting that even people paying for the Xbox cloud streaming service will encounter wait times during peak hours, though the blog post stated these waits will be shorter.

Microsoft previously revealed that monthly time limits will be placed on its paid Xbox cloud gaming service, though it insisted only a fraction of players would run into this cut-off point. A report claimed a 15-hour cap placed on the Game Pass Ultimate cloud gaming service was present as that's the moment Xbox starts losing money. Offering a cloud gaming service requires server infrastructure, compute costs, and network and bandwidth costs.

As an aside, Sony's defunct cloud gaming service PlayStation Now used to charge $9.99 for a month of streamed game time, more than a decade ago.

Xbox is currently in the midst of a massive restructuring process, in which more than 3,000 employees are to be laid off from the company. In a recent report, additional waves of layoffs are said to be planned for later this month, November, and January.

#4095. Phantom Blade Zero Is an Instant Hit with 4 Million Sales on PS5, PC

Phantom Blade Zero sold over four million copies during its first three days on the market across PS5 and PC, studio S-GAME has announced.

Having released on 29th October 2026, the new action game achieved the milestone by the end of the weekend. "Thank you everyone from the bottom of our hearts for all the love and support," the developer said on social media.

The game is only available digitally for now on PS5 and PC, but three physical editions are launching in 2027.

Review Phantom Blade Zero (PS5) - One of the Generation's Greatest Action Experiences

As a new title out of China, the most obvious comparison point here is Black Myth: Wukong. It managed to sell over 10 million copies in the same three-day launch period, so Phantom Blade Zero hasn't managed even half of that.

That's not to take away from the S-GAME effort: four million sales in three days is still a very noteworthy achievement — Black Myth: Wukong is just an anomaly. With very strong reviews and word of mouth from players, I expect that sales will continue at a good pace in the coming weeks and months.

The social media post focuses on user scores (9.3 on Metacritic and 4.71 on the PS Store), but critics have turned in an average of 87 on PS5 (88 on PC). In my own Phantom Blade Zero PS5 review, I said:

"An intense and fast-paced combat system is the star, with so much variety backing it and incredible enemies to test it. Fun exploration, beautiful visuals, and a unique style then help it reach the heights of the genre’s elite, as Phantom Blade Zero deserves to hang with the best of the best."

#4094. Mass Effect 3 ending discourse ignored the RPG's scale, ambition, and exuberance, including that of its oddly great co-op

Ah, come on, it was fine. Better than fine. We can argue for another fourteen years about whether BioWare should have redone the ending or not, but Mass Effect 3 was really a compendium of endings, a ludicrously ambitious wrapping-up of dozens of plot threads, character arcs, and running gags. Even if you can point to other RPGs that, on an individual basis, are more branching and reactive, Mass Effect 3's largely successful closing of a galaxy's worth of choose-your-own adventure books - filled in and followed across three evolving instalments - showed an audacity and grandiosity that no other three-part series had matched before. Or, at least on that scale, has pulled off since.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

It didn't hurt that Mass Effect 3 also had the trilogy's fiercest, bangiest action by far, nor some of its highest-stakes, often most lip-chewing moments of decisionmaking. It is true that the accumulation of War Assets wasn't always as heavy on character drama as the game-long preparation for Mass Effect 2's Suicide Mission, but then you don't simply play Mass Effect 3 to make a number go higher. You play it to punch or hug reporters, to love or shoot your friends, to save or damn entire species. And it has loads of that, right up to the point to have to choose the colour of an explosion. Potentially beyond, if you treat the (assuredly, delightfully) fanservice-forward Citadel expansion as Shepard's true last ride.

Back in 2013, and again with 2021's Legendary Edition, I was sad that Mass Effect 3 ended and glad that it happened. That, at the risk of appearing less furious at EA's stewardship than I am, does not change with BioWare's closure. What does bother me is the uncertainty over what now happens to Mass Effect 3's surprisingly entertaining, weirdly long-lived co-op mode.

I don't doubt this was put in for boring, C-suite, "gamers want multiplayer" reasons. But that only gave the resultant palled-up superpower maelstroms a sense that they were better than they had any right to be, with explosive moments of player-to-player power synergies and spacious, blindspot-filled maps that could maintain a thrilling feeling of being permanently surrounded. Post-release additions to the species-spanning character roster also showed glimpses of that same, fuck-it swagger that BioWare exhibited in the campaign, as they increasingly moved away from familiar soldier archtypes towards electric whip wielders, regenerating lizards, teleporting ninjas, and three-foot-tall psychic asthmatics. While many of today's co-op shooters fret over miniscule balance changes, in pursuit of some mythically perfect meta, Mass Effect 3's gave you a crate of action figures and told you to go nuts.

While I haven't played it recently, there's a small but loyal contingent who do, and for their sake I hope the multiplayer's P2P setup helps it survive the EA cull. I was, and for now technically still is, too good to be doomed to oblivion. Or, worse, vibe-coded Legendary Edition mods.

#4093. Poll: So, How Many Xbox Mythic Achievements Do You Have So Far?

Xbox's Platinum Trophy equivalent was made public earlier this week, and it's been exciting to see just how many Mythic Achievements we've unlocked since we first picked up an Xbox 360 controller.

Mythic Achievements are an additional reward for unlocking all of a game's base achievements to reach 100% completion. As it stands, Pure Xbox Editor Fraser Gilbert is rocking 8 Mythics, with the likes of FIFA 14, Rocket League, and a bunch of Telltale's The Walking Dead games. Whereas, Staff Writer Craig Reid picked up 36 Mythics playing titles such as Alan Wake II, Signalis, End of Abyss, and the wonderful, Duck Detective: The Ghost of Glamping.

Craig is currently toying with the idea of starting a new "Become Mythic" feature. The idea is to post an article for every Mythic earned, describing what it was like to unlock the achievement, talk about the game a little bit, and to see how many he can get in a year. It's not an original concept - in fact, it's inspired by our sister site Push Square's 'Going Platinum' feature written by the lovely Stephen Tailby.

We think these new full-completion accolades are a very smart addition to the Xbox console experience, and we'd really like to know just how many our lovely Pure Xbox community has.

So, let's hear it, gang! Tell us how many Mythic Achievements you have by voting in the poll below, as well as sharing your most favourite Mythic'd game in the comments section.

#4092. Following shock BioWare closure, scope of EA job cuts becomes clear as layoffs hit Respawn, Maxis, Full Circle, EA Motive, and more

EA announced overnight it's closing Mass Effect and Dragon Age studio BioWare in a new round of cuts that include the elimination of 400 roles across the publisher. But while it confirmed BioWare's 50 workers are affected, and that Skate studio Ripple Effect was being downsized, it did not say where the other 350 job cuts would come from.

Now, however, new information has emerged revealing The Sims studio Maxis, Battlefield support studio Ripple Effect, and EA Motive are all impacted by layoffs, alongside Full Circle and BioWare. That's according to Vertical Slice, citing an "anonymous source" supported by corroborating information on LinkedIn.

Maxis senior director Anna Huerta and three Ripple Effect artists - Brandon Garcia, Corey Thomas, and Turner Spring - confirmed their departure from EA on LinkedIn. Catheryn Grant, operations product manager at both Ripple Effect and Respawn, also revealed she was among those impacted, as was EA Motive's senior gameplay designer Jamieson Shearer. Full Circle's senior designer David Milne and seasonal creative director John Epler are affected too.

In a memo to staff shared overnight, EA said it had paused development of an unannounced Sims project called Project Lotus in order to focus on a different title dubbed Project Evergreen. The company also said it was downsizing Full Circle to "create an experience that keeps [players] engaged over the long-term", so there was already some suggestion those studios would face job cuts.

More surprising, though, are the cuts at Respawn, a studio EA said it would be investing "heavily" in to support the growth of free-to-play shooter Apex Legends. Respawn is also co-developing a new project alongside DICE, which is reportedly Star Wars: Battlefront 3. By the same token, EA said it's throwing its "full weight behind" Motive Studio's Iron Man game and Respawn's Star Wars Jedi sequel, its only two action-adventure projects currently in the works.

This is the first round of layoffs at EA since the company was fully acquired by a consortium made up of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, investment firm Silver Lake, and private equity company Affinity Partners earlier this year. The trio acquired EA in the summer for $55bn in one of the largest leveraged buyout deals ever.

When the deal closed, EA told debt investors it would cut $700m in annual costs, including $170m in "organisational efficiencies". At the time, many feared that would translate to major layoffs.

Co-showrunner Patrick McKay says The Rings of Power season 3's five-year time jump allowed "the world to change"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's only been two real years since The Lord of the Rings prequel was on our screens, but five years will have passed when The Rings of Power season 3 picks up. However, showrunner Patrick McKay says the break has allowed Middle-earth to reach the point where war is brewing again, so we can dive right back into the action.

"The five-year jump allowed the story to have scope, for the world to change,” said co‑showrunner Patrick McKay in an interview with SFX Magazine. "The war has been raging across Middle-earth, and now we’re at a tipping point. Sauron has conquered everything except for two pockets of Elven resistance that are defended by their rings."

McKay continued, "This third season is where every single storyline becomes part of the large, epic war between Sauron and the Elves, and hopefully the show is deeper in its emotionality and the psychology of the characters."

Season 2 ended with the Dark Lord on top after killing Celebrimbor and securing the Nine Rings of Men. The Elves took another hit when Eregion fell under seige, leading the surviving Elves to flee to what will become known as Rivendell. Elsewhere, the Stranger was finally revealed as Gandalf, and Balrog was freed. From that point on, all sides have been preparing for war, as season 3 promises a fiery battle. Perhaps this is why McKay told SFX that The Rings of Power "hits its stride" in season 3.

According to the official synopsis from Amazon, we know that in the time that has passed, Sauron’s armies have started their march toward our heroes, with just a few sites left standing. That includes Khazad-dûm, where the Dwarves are sealed deep in the mountains, and the elven realms of Lindon and Rivendell. Now, Sauron sits in his tower in Mordor, growing even more enraged with the desire for domination. The Elves, Dwarves, Free Men, and Wizards must come together to prevent him from forging The One Ring to Rule Them All.

Season 3 welcomes back Morfydd Clark as Galadriel, Charlie Vickers as Sauron, and Daniel Weyman as Gandalf, and adds Jamie Campbell Bower as Galadriel's long-lost love, Celeborn.

The Rings of Power season 3 hits Prime Video on November 11. For more, check out our guides on how to watch The Lord of the Rings movies and shows in order and the Lord of the Rings timeline.

#4090. Games industry mourns sudden BioWare closure - "Anyone who participated in this travesty should be ashamed"

"I would have never been here without BioWare igniting the fire in my heart."

Following the sudden closure of Bioware last night, people from across the games industry have shared their sympathies for those employees losing their jobs, and said farewell to one of the most influential RPG developers of all time.

The reactions come in many forms, with BioWare staff throughout the years looking back on their time at the studio and thanking their peers and fans for support. Game developers from other studios have paid tribute too, sharing their own tales of how Bioware impacted their careers.

"As much as it's not really a surprise," former Dragon age lead writer David Gaider on Bluesky, "especially given the industry right now coupled with the Saudi sale, the news today still made me sad ... BioWare joins other great studios of the past, with a legacy that will not soon be forgotten."

Former Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age lead James Ohlen also paid tribute to the studio, writing: "BioWare is closing. My 22 years there made me the man I am. The people affected today are some of the best RPG developers in the world. If you're hiring writers, designers, artists or engineers, start with them. Former BioWare folks: if an intro from me would help, reach out."

"This is sad news on multiple fronts," former Mass Effect boss and one-time BioWare general manager Casey Hudson added on X, "for those of us who worked there, for our friends and colleagues at BioWare who are impacted, and for fans who were looking forward to the next Mass Effect adventure.

"I started my career at BioWare and will forever be grateful to the founders, Greg and Ray, for inviting me to join in BioWare's legendary journey. Its legacy will live on through those who were part of it and continue to create games through a passion for unforgettable stories, worlds and characters."

"Remember BioWare is 100% owned by EA,” said Mark Darrah, former Dragon Age and Anthem executive producer in a YouTube video. “EA owns all the IPs. They own Dragon Age, they own Mass Effect, they own Jade Empire. That doesn’t change the situation, really, at all. [...] Now, there’s nobody working on a [BioWare] game, or games, within the EA organization, and chances are there never will be, which might make them more likely to sell off those IPs. But it might also make them more likely to just try to forget that they ever existed and bury them in the vault."

Trick Weekes, former narrative designer on the Mass Effect and Dragon Age series, posted a video from Mass Effect 3's Citadel DLC, in which Commander Shepard and their crew say a sombre farewell, while actor Mark Meer, the voice of male Shepard, shared his condolences and thanks with BioWare staff past and present.

Michael Gamble, who served as project director on the now-cancelled Mass Effect 5 until yesterday's layoffs also took to social media, thanking people for their support during his 17 years at the company, saying it "has meant everything to me."

While BioWare's closure prompted many studio alumni to share their thoughts, an outpouring of support and mourning came from outside the company too. "This is not something I ever expected to see," Swen Vincke, CEO of Baldur's Gate 3 developer Larian, wrote on social media. "Larian and Bioware started their trajectories in the games industry at the same time and Bioware led the way in making RPGs big. It's almost unimaginable that we're now entering an era where the name BioWare won't show up anymore when discussing upcoming RPGs. What a loss for all of us."

CD Projekt Red co-studio head Michał Nowakowski also recalled how important BioWare was to the Polish studio. "Bioware has been a massive part of CDPR history," he wrote. "We befriended them when localising and selling Baldur’s Gate games in Poland, Czech, and Slovakia. And later they were [a] great help when lending us their engine for Witcher 1, sharing their wisdom and even giving us a spot at their booth at E3. I had [the] pleasure to visit them a few times in Edmonton and also host them in our Warsaw office. Very sad for the people affected, but also sad to see a legendary brand go down. Not a great day in the games industry."

"Thank you for all the games. Thank you for the many hours of gameplay. Thank you for all the stories . You can be damned proud of what you achieved. I hope you all land well."

Nowakowski was joined by his peer Paweł Sasko, associate director of CD Projekt's upcoming Cyberpunk sequel, who revealed the importance of BioWare's games on his own career: "Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 shaped my imagination and the desire to create games. I would have never been here without BioWare igniting the fire in my heart. It inspired me, formed me, enriched my imagination, and for that I will be forever grateful. I will always remember you."

Dave Gilbert, founder of Old Skies and The Blackwell Legacy studio Wadjet Eye Games, similarly spoke of BioWare's impact on his career: "Eff me. Not Bioware, too. This one hurts more than most. I can't think of a studio that has had a bigger influence on me than this one. My dream was to be like them. I'll never stop feeling angry when studios with tremendous legacies just get bought and killed off for parts."

Some too had harsh words for EA and those behind Bioware's closure, alongside sympathy for those affected. Legendary immersive sim developer Warren Spector, for instance, decried the fact the development team had now been left "out in the cold with so many others."

"BioWare is more than just another studio," he continued. "For decades it’s played a central role in the history of our medium. They, for many years, as effectively as any studio, married art and commerce. Their work changed things. This is such bad news, such a devastating historic event all I can say is that it’s utter bullshit. Anyone who participated in this travesty should be ashamed.

"Actually, maybe all of the people who participated — the folks in suits (real or virtual) should lose their damn jobs. I ask them to ponder this: What do you contribute to gaming? What price do you pay for failure? I’d love to see THEM on the unemployment line instead of the people who do real work. Why is it always the do-ers and makers who pay the price? Someone explain that to me!"

Following news of BioWare's closure, EA confirmed other sweeping changes across the company, which will result in a total of 400 job cuts. While it did not explicitly name the other studios impacted by the move, employees have already started posting on social media, revealing the likes of Respawn, Maxis, Full Circle, EA Motive, and Ripple Effect have all been impacted. The layoffs come after EA was fully acquired by a consortium made up of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, investment firm Silver Lake, and private equity company Affinity Partners for $55bn earlier this year.

Eurogamer wishes all those impacted by the layoffs the very best for the future.

#4089. I've got egg on my face because Steam's Personal Calendar feature has apparently been a test this whole time and is only now actually a fully fledged component

I'll be honest folks: I didn't know that Steam's Personal Calendar feature was still technically in testing. I've been using it here and there to keep track of what's come out recently or what's coming out imminently, and have generally found it to be fairly reflective of the kinds of games I was interested in. It just worked! Yet lo and behold, a post from Valve went out yesterday announcing that the feature has launched out of Steam Labs "and is considered a full feature of the Steam Store."

The feature, if you've missed it, is "another way to see recommended games for you, showing both recently released and upcoming games filtered down to the set of games we think you are most likely to be interested in," as Valve explain it anyway. "It uses your recently played games to find people with similar playtime profiles to you, and then looks at the games those players have been adding to their wishlist or playing." I do wonder if there's a bit more going under the hood here, as my playtime count is all over the place, with nothing above 50 hours on there, and that's an exception to the norm (I'm from more of a console background, alright).

But even still, my recommendations do remain pretty good, showing me games that I have since added to my wishlist. I'm never opposed to new discovery tools, especially considering how bad Valve can actually be at that kind of thing. Apparently the recommendation system refreshes daily "to incorporate the latest data. In reality you aren't likely to see your recommendations change all that much from day to day, but as time goes by you will obviously see new things pop up as the 8-week horizon of the calendar marches forward, or as games lock in their release dates."

This comes as part of a broader swathe of changes Valve have been introducing to Steam over the past couple of years, including one from last month that will change its homepage discounts and events section to be a bit more algorithm based. Perhaps it's some kind of weird prepwork for that new Half-Life they're almost definitely making but only talk about accidentally.

#4088. Despite its mixed reception, Marvel's Wolverine was September's top-selling new game in the US, making Sony launch revenues it hasn't seen since Helldivers 2

Marvel's Wolverine may not have had the best critical reception, but that clearly didn't discourage consumers. The action-adventure from Marvel's Spider-Man studio Insomniac has topped US video game sales in September, despite releasing exactly halfway through the month.

That's according to market analysis firm Circana, which noted Wolverine's success includes digital sales and those made at retail. It was such a hit that, as Circana analyst Mat Piscatella wrote, the game delivered "the highest launch month dollar sales" a Sony-published game has seen since Helldivers 2, which released in February 2024. It is worth noting, however, that Helldivers 2 launched on PC alongside PlayStation 5, while Wolverine is a PS5 exclusive. Additionally, Helldivers 2 had a much lower price of $40 compared to Wolverine's $70, meaning the former sold more copies to arrive at a similar point.

Wolverine seemingly helped boost PS5 sales, too, as the console saw a massive 43 percent uptick in dollar sales compared to the same period last year, though some of that is owed to its higher price now compared to then. In fact, PS5 led the month in both unit sales (up 22 percent from last year) and dollar sales across consoles. Switch 2 unit sales fell by 14 percent and Xbox by 27 percent - according to Circana, that means Xbox unit sales dropped to their lowest ever in a September, claiming the record from September 2025.

September, of course, was one of the busiest months for games this year, and that was reflected in the top-ten, which saw eight new releases - including The Blood of Dawnwalker, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Switch 2-exclusive Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, and PC-exclusive Wardogs. Also among those was NBA 2K27, which, despite failing to claim the top spot in September, surprisingly managed to dethrone Resident Evil Requiem to become the best-selling game this year so far - a record it surely can't hold on to for long with GTA 6 on the horizon.

Circana's most interesting report this year is undoubtedly going to be November's, when GTA 6 arrives, but October's should also be eye-opening, because it's Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's release month, the other major release of 2026.

#4087. Three Xbox Games Are Shutting Down Their Servers In November & December 2026

A few notable delistings on the way as well

November has officially arrived, and therefore we thought we'd bring you our latest roundup of games getting delisted over the next few weeks, with this roundup specifically focusing on November and December 2026.

The good news is that there's not much to talk about! Call of Duty: Warzone is undoubtedly the most notable of the bunch here, which has been set to go offline on Xbox One and PS4 for some time. They originally announced that it would go offline when Modern Warfare 4 Season 1 began, and that's now officially set for November 6th, 2026.

Beyond that, NBA 2K25 is losing its servers at the end of the year, while Synduality: Echo of Ada is turning off its in-game purchases in December ahead of a planned full server closure in May of 2027.

Beyond this, we also wanted to bring your attention to Amazon's New World: Aeternum, which is officially shutting down its servers at the end of January 2027. We'll remind you again nearer the time, but it's worth being aware of it now too!

As for upcoming delistings, both Street Outlaws and Street Outlaws 2 will disappear off the Xbox Store at the end of December 2026, so you'll need to buy them before then if you want the ability to re-download them in the future.

We've seen on many occasions that announcements like these can spring up at the last minute, so we'll keep an eye out and let you know of any big reveals over the next couple of months. For now though, the damage doesn't look too bad!

As IT: Welcome to Derry season 2 stays in preproduction, HBO keeps fans fed with a secret Halloween episode

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Do you remember when Stranger Things fans convinced themselves that a secret ninth episode was on the way earlier this year? Well, although we never did get to go back to Hawkins, another beloved franchise has taken its fanbase by surprise and delivered a secret instalment, allowing fans to return back to Derry almost one year after IT: Welcome to Derry season 1 came to an end.

Without any warning, HBO randomly released the 30-minute-long bonus episode, titled 'A Story of Derry,' on Halloween. Set hundreds of years before Pennywise came to be, the new episode follows three youngsters from a Native American tribe who venture into the Western Wood where they encounter a terrifying ancient spirit. HBO Max shared a short trailer for the special on Twitter, which you can watch below.

IT's a surprise Halloween treat. Catch this never-before-seen special exploring the origins of IT in Derry. #AStoryOfDerry is streaming now on HBO Max. 🎈 https://t.co/NH3NcMLt8nOctober 31, 2026

The new episode gives us more insight into what the evil entity we know as IT actually is and why it targets Derry. However, we got a little taste of this in IT: Welcome to Derry season 1. In episode 4, after Dick Hallorann enters Taniel's mind, he learns that the Native Americans stumbled upon the entity, which they call 'Tha Gallo,' many years ago when they settled on the land. Tha Gallo murdered tribe members and would grow stronger with every kill, so the natives imprisoned it beneath a large area that would later become the town of Derry.

The special brings Dick's vision to life and reveals just how the natives caged the beast. We already know that the spirit was kept at bay by a number of pillars placed around the forest, which is why it can never leave Derry and break out into the wider world. However, the caveat is that IT wakes every 27 years and causes a catastrophic event in Derry before it sleeps again. IT: Welcome to Derry season 1 takes place in the '60s, 27 years before the first IT movie, which in turn takes place 27 years before IT: Chapter 2.

IT: Welcome to Derry season 2 is set to take us right back to the 1930s. Just as season 1 saw the monster feed on the horrific Black Spot disaster, season 2 is set around another tragic event: the Bradley Gang Massacre. Mentioned in Stephen King's 1986 novel, the event sees a band of criminals target stores and banks in Derry, which leads to a deadly shootout in the middle of town. Season 2 is currently in the pre-production stage, with Crystal Lake creator Brad Caleb Kane serving as solo showrunner this time.

It: Welcome to Derry season 2 does not yet have a release date. For more, check out our list of the best shows on HBO Max, and keep up with upcoming Stephen King movies and shows on the way.

#4085. Yakuza Creator's Gang of Dragon PS5 Game and New Studio Officially Dead

Gang of Dragon, the Yakuza-esque title Toshiro Nagoshi planned to make with a newly set-up developer under NetEase, will never see the light of day. Nagoshi Studio has now officially been closed, as of 31st October 2026.

This news had been expected for some time, as reports dating back to March 2026 detail publisher NetEase pulling its funding. The game had only been revealed a few months prior at The Game Awards. Now we know for sure the studio and PS5 game are both gone, as a notice has appeared in the Japanese government gazette Kanpo (via Gematsu).

Nagoshi Studio was dissolved by a shareholders' resolution, as of 31st October 2026.

Past reports have claimed NetEase stopped funding the project after it was revealed that another ¥7 billion (~$44 million) would be required to finish Gang of Dragon and bring it to market. The publisher has been scaling back its international video game efforts, and Nagoshi Studio fell victim to those cuts.

At the time of reveal, Gang of Dragon was pitched as a melee-based action-adventure title set in Shinjuku, Tokyo. "Shin Ji-seong — portrayed by renowned Asian actor Ma Dong-seok — is a high-ranking member of a Korean crime syndicate based in Kabukicho. As he explores the streets of Shinjuku, Shin becomes entangled in underworld conflicts and forges intense, human connections that push him to confront his own sense of purpose."

That work will now never see the light of day.

#4084. BioWare's cancelled Mass Effect game would've learned from Baldur's Gate 3 and The Witcher to deliver "a level of autonomy and choice that no other game has"

"I'm sad you won't ever get to see what we were cooking."

EA has closed its longtime studio partner BioWare, the iconic development house behind Mass Effect and Dragon Age, impacting around 50 staff who were in pre-production on the next Mass Effect game. In the aftermath of EA's decision, one of those affected has shared a little about the project, claiming it would have featured unprecedented levels of player freedom and choice reactivity.

Tony de Waal, a BioWare veteran who has worked on previous Mass Effect and Dragon Age games, offered a rare look behind the scenes at what the team was attempting. In a LinkedIn post (via PC Gamer), de Waal suggested the studio wanted to surpass the acclaimed work of the role-playing giants at Baldur's Gate 3 studio Larian and CD Projekt Red, maker of The Witcher and Cyberpunk.

"I was one of the lucky ones who stayed with BioWare to start on the next Mass Effect, where I believe we were making something special: a level of autonomy and choice that no other game has been able to match," de Waal wrote. "We saw what Larian and CD Projekt were bringing to the table with their latest offerings, and started down a path to bring Mass Effect to the next level while remaining true to the trilogy," he added.

The veteran cinematics lead sadly didn't offer any examples of what that could've looked like in-game, but given previous Mass Effect games have incorporated a great deal of player freedom, the idea of a sequel that builds on that - while incorporating modern techniques from CDPR and Larian - would certainly have been exciting.

"I'm sad you won't ever get to see what we were cooking, and sad for the small, talented group of devs who were all punching above their weight to make something special," de Waal continued. "Please consider those who stayed with BioWare until the very end. They are truly some of the most talented people I've had the pleasure of working with throughout my career."

BioWare's closure feels sudden; it was only a year ago the studio stressed its new Mass Effect game remains in development. At the time, EA's private acquisition had just been announced. The $55bn sale has since been approved, freeing EA to start making cuts many suspected were coming.

More broadly, the move also signals an end to EA's interest in developing deep role-playing games. Outside of its sports and shooter series, EA's non-casual projects are an unannounced Star Wars Jedi sequel, and the Marvel's Iron Man game we've yet to see.

#4083. Paralives' first major update slips to next year, but when it comes you can expect some pretty meaty improvements for all of its main features

Since launch back in May of this year, life sim Paralives appears to have been trucking along nicely, with the dev team offering up fairly regular updates with all sorts of tweaks big and small. Certainly confidence-inspiring for an early access game, especially one as systems-driven as it is. And now, the Paralives team have outlined their plans for the game's first major update, which seem very catered to improving the core experience.

As part of a four point plan they outlined, first up on the docket is "buffing up the basics." This is all about strengthening some of the currently existing Live Mode systems. That means improvements to how relationships function by unlocking more things when a relationship level goes up, adding in more interactions that change your Para's emotions, improving the Community Centre's bundles and tweaking the economy curve so it isn't as easy to get money.

The next point is on expanding the Live Mode, meaning the addition of a pair of new skills, adding in more together and story cards, new relationship label unlockables, and more jobs too. Build Mode will also see some improvements, with a big focus on build breaking bugs. You can also expect new bits of furniture and items, and a tweak to furniture and item efficiency.

Lastly, there are also planned improvements to the Paramaker. One is by adding in more hairstyles and clothing items, notably baggy outfits, and the other is increasing the range of fat and muscle sliders "to represent a wider variety of body shapes." As a bigger person myself I'm always enthused when character creators actually let you have a fat body, so this is a welcome point from the dev team.

Worth noting that this list "is not final," and some things may be pushed back with others getting added in. Also worth noting is that while this first major update was planned for the end of 2026, it's been pushed into next year as the team needs a bit more time. You can read about all of these plans in more detail over on Steam.

#4082. Final Fantasy 14, Umamusume: Pretty Derby, and more impacted as PHP vulnerability outages hit games around the globe

Multiple games - including Final Fantasy 14 and Umamusume: Pretty Derby - have faced outages and other issues following this week's discovery of a serious PHP vulnerability.

This vulnerability could potentially result in substantial security breaches for the massive number of websites and applications built using the PHP programming language. As a result, it was advised that online services built upon it should be taken offline until a fix could be distributed and applied. Inevitably, games were caught up.

An official post made to the Final Fantasy 14 lodestone website informed users that security "enhancements" were being made to the MMO's patch servers. As a result, new logins were temporarily disabled until the updates could be completed. While logins have since been turned back on, the server back-up feature for user's save data remains offline.

Horse racing gacha game Umamusume: Pretty Derby, meanwhile, was taken offline completely. As its server-side infrastructure uses PHP, a sudden maintenance outage was put in place - though its developer assured players no exploitation of the security vulnerability had occurred. Right now, Japanese and global servers are back online, with a compensatory package of in-game currency being sent to all players.

Path of Titans, an in-beta dinosaur MMO (which sounds awesome by the way) is still down as of writing. In an announcement made to its official X account, developer Alderon Games explained the MMOand its website had been taken down for up to three days as a precautionary measure. Players were also assured no data had been compromised.

One hopes the chaos is largely over now a fix is in circulation. But even if it is, the fact that so many services all across the globe - far beyond the games industry - have rushed to protect the sanctity of their data and that of their users speaks to the seriousness of the situation. Take a moment to thank the tech heads out there who may have had to work around the clock to get this sorted.

A 4K remaster of Spaced is on the way, but Edgar Wright doesn't approve

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new 4K remaster of classic British comedy series Spaced is on the way, but it seems like someone wished for it on a monkey's paw, as it's been upscaled using "algorithmic corrections" and none of the show's original creators are involved, including Edgar Wright.

Responding to a fan on X, Wright confirmed that the 4K release of Spaced, which is currently up for pre-order on Amazon UK, was news to him and fellow Spaced alumni, like Simon Pegg and Nick Frost. "Finding out about this for the first time is... disheartening," Wright posted on X. "I had been pushing to do a Blu-Ray of SPACED for years, so to find out that someone just went ahead without our involvement is.... a bummer. Not authorized by anyone involved in making the show. Finding out what happened as we speak…"

To make matters worse, the Amazon listing confirms that the show, which ran from 1999-2001 and was shot on standard definition DigiBeta cameras, was upscaled to 4K using a proprietary AI algorithm. British label All3 Media is behind the release.

"This global first Blu-Ray collection," reads the Amazon listing, "has been upgraded to a brand new 4K master using a combination of traditional and proprietary tools in a multi-step process of non-commercial and algorithmic corrections that are additionally enhanced frame by frame by a manual operator – guaranteeing the most state-of-the-art upconversion possible." That's a whole lot of words not to say AI…

Spaced was one of the early great DVD boxsets, featuring hours of special features involving Cornetto trilogy pals Wright, Pegg, Frost and many famous fans (Diablo Cody, Kevin Smith and Matt Stone all contribute to the commentary tracks), but for reasons currently unclear, this new edition won't feature any new contributions from those who made it.

"It’s a Channel 4 show," Wright pointed out when asked how this could happen without his knowledge. "We were all very involved in the previous editions, but not this one."

The 4K remaster of Spaced releases on February 27, 2027 in the UK, though whether you'll want to pick it up is another question. As for Wright, we don't know what the Baby Driver and Last Night in Soho director is working on next, though his partner in crime Simon Pegg did confirm earlier this year that he and Wright are working on a new film together, telling Something About Rocks, "Edgar and I are, at the moment, meeting up weekly either in person or on Zoom, just to talk about ideas. We’ve got a lot of potential avenues to walk down."

Spaced can currently be streamed on Channel 4 in the UK. For more, dive into our list of upcoming TV shows or upcoming movies.

#4080. Smash Bros. director Masahiro Sakurai thinks gen-AI will cause a surge of unoriginal games, but says human creativity can't be replicated

Masahiro Sakurai has spoken about the pitfalls of generative AI use in game development, saying that while he believes the technology will result in a surge of unoriginal video games, human creativity - such as that shown by designers like Ico's Fumito Ueda - can't be replicated.

In an interview with Japanese news outlet Denfaminicogamer, Sakurai was asked about his time judging for the Game Designers Awards (a role he recently retired from) and his thoughts on the massive increase of game releases since the awards began. In 2010, 275 games were published on Steam, whereas more than 19,000 released this year.

"19,000 is amazing, but I think that number will increase even more from now on," Sakurai said (as translated from Japanese using Google Translate). "I'm sure of it. That's because AI will increase the number. However, I think most of them will become 'unprofitable titles'. There are too many to keep track of, and it's impossible to understand them all.

"When it comes to things created with AI... or things mass-produced with poor quality, I think most of them will simply be reproductions of systems seen in various other games. I think there are already a lot of those now."

Sakurai then spoke about a recent (and lovely) release called Librarian: Tidy Up the Arcane Library!, which challenges players to organise books on shelves, and pointed to other puzzle games with similarly simple premises, such as finding a needle in a haystack or organising a supermarket. These kinds of games, he suggested, will be very easy for AI to replicate.

We've already seen this happen, of course. Needle in a Haystack Simulator, for example - which asks players to find a needle buried among 5 million pieces of hay - went viral thanks to its absurd yet compelling premise. Following its surge in popularity, copies were quickly created, prompting Needle in a Haystack developer Studio Bitdot to plop a bright red "original" tag on its Steam artwork.

But Sakurai continued, saying generative AI may become powerful enough to replicate more complicated games, like acclaimed designer Fumito Ueda's Ico or Shadow of the Colossus. However, he emphasised that Ueda's future games will be "something that AI simply cannot replicate ... What kind of artistic style will his future works possess? That's something only he can create. I think that's where human creativity lies."

"Basically, AI refers to things that have been created so far, but it can't refer to things that haven't been created before," Sakurai elaborated. "I think this is true not only for AI, but for various kinds of creative works as well.

"I wouldn't go so far as to call them 'pioneers', but rather people who forge their own path... people who understand and can create their own unique flavour... will become increasingly important from now on. I think this is especially true in an era of mass production and low-quality goods."

Quickly made AI games have become an increasing presence in the games industry of late. Valve's current Steam Next Fest features more than double the number of demos compared to last year, due in part to the influx of 'AI slop'. Some indie developers have even pulled planned demos and playtests out of fear their games might be copied by AI before they're properly released.

#4079. HELENA : Cloud District is a megastructure photography game laser targeted at my interests, and it's out next week

Yes, I'm doing it, I'm writing about a megastructure game for the second time this week because come on, HELENA : Cloud District just looks stunning, don't it? Admittedly there's a chance you've not heard of it, that be the way of things in this algorithmically dominated world, but allow me to tell you about its big, scary world and the strange camera you're equipped with to capture all the sights it holds.

In the world of HELENA : Cloud District, you have come across a rotting megastructure that appears to be long abandoned, all sorts of strange flora dotted throughout it. In one part, it's something of a precision first-person platformer, as you navigate its intricately layered world with drops so steep you'd probably die before you hit the bottom. At the centre of it all is a computer, and it's here where you must bring all of your photographs in order to learn more about the history of the place.

The in-game camera itself is a fascinating thing to look at, completely impossible, alien and ancient in its design. From what I can tell it's a sort of metallic helmet, these insect-like segments snapping into place when you're gearing up to take a snap. You only appear to have three photo slots at any given point in time, meaning you can't just go gallivanting around the place all trigger happy like. There's an amount of care you have to put in positioning yourself and subsequently finding your way back to the central computer.

It's non-linear too, there's no set path you have to take, and it seems like there's some neat movement mechanics too. "Slide, hover, and glide through the structure in your own creative way in order to reach every level and get deeper into the slumbering Cloud District," explains the game's Steam page. Sounds like you don't have to worry too much about that falling to your death thing, then. I'm quite enthused by what HELENA : Cloud District is putting down, and it has a release date now too: October 29th. Same day as Hypnos! I now dub October 29th megastructure day. There will not be a vote on this matter. Ahead of HELENA's release, make sure to give it a wishlist on Steam.

#4078. Flashy internal trailer for now-cancelled Mass Effect Universe appears online, following EA's closure of BioWare

An internal trailer for the cancelled Mass Effect game that was in-development at BioWare prior to its closure this week has appeared online. It's confirmed to be real, too, amid some initial suspicions it may have been an AI generated fake.

The trailer was intended for internal use, and was created for EA leadership rather than the public. It starts with a short message: "The following is in-engine footage from our small team. It uses our pre-production assets."

The trailer shows us our first (and likely only) look at Mass Effect Universe, an entirely new entry following the adventures of a new protagonist. We see them navigate the galaxy in their own ship with a new crew of various known races including a Krogan, and get into fights using guns and biotics. There's some quick cuts to a saucy romance scene, a tense standoff with weapons drawn, and a mysterious creature being researched in a big test tube. We also see a returning character from the original trilogy - Liara - make an appearance near the end of the trailer before a big bar fight kicks off.

When first released, scepticism around whether this trailer was real naturally was present given the prevalence of AI, however IGN quickly verified its validity. In addition, Bloomberg's Jason Schrier went on to corroborate the trailer's authenticity on his personal BlueSky account.

We know very little about this game aside from this trailer. According to a former BioWare employee, Mass Effect Universe would have learned from Baldur's Gate 3 and The Witcher to deliver "a level of autonomy and choice that no other game has." The game would have also seemingly "remained true" to the original trilogy.

Reactions from this trailer are bittersweet, given the reality that the 50 developers working on Mass Effect Universe have recently lost their jobs as part of EA's layoffs which impacted 400 employees across the company. "A spy thriller is such a cool concept for a re-entry to the series," wrote Reddit user Harrywilko. "Man, I'm just so sad and angry." User TerraxFormer shared similar sentiments, writing: "God this makes me even more distraught lol. I know a trailer is not an indication of how good it would have been but I was looking forward to this damn game so much."

The EA job cuts, which took place only a few months after Saudi Arabia's $55bn leveraged buyout of the company, also hit developers at Respawn, Maxis, Full Circle, EA Motive, and other EA-owned studios. While such cuts were anticipated by experts given EA's new debt obligations, the news of BioWare's closure nonetheless drew out many messages of sympathy and anger from across the industry.

It's hardly a silver lining, given we saw this unfinished trailer while we all said a sad farewell to BioWare. But at least those staff can know they were onto something that could have been great.
